newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-HAVELANGE SAYS HE TREATED PELE LIKE A SON.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HAVELANGE SAYS HE TREATED PELE LIKE A SON.

text.p: FIFA president Joao Havelange claimed a large dose of credit on Thursday for helping Pele become the world's greatest soccer player.

Havelange also announced he will leave his successor around $4 billion in the coffers when he retires next year, claimed he never slept more than five hours a night and had spent 87 hours on aircraft in the last three weeks.

The 80-year-old Brazilian has become locked in a battle with Pele over a bill that the legendary former player, acting in his new capacity as his country's sports minister, had introduced in an attempt to reform Brazilian football.
If approved, Pele's bill would drastically reduce the power of the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF), which is headed by Havelange's son-in-law Ricardo Teixeira.
Havelange has replied by warning that, by interfering in the CBF, the bill infringes on FIFA statutes and that if it is approved, Brazil could be suspended and even miss out on next year's World Cup.

"I was in Hong Kong recently and I was offered a banquet in my honour," said Havelange, who spent much of a conference with foreign journalists in Rio de Janeiro extolling his own virtues. "That's why I am hurt when I am criticised in my own country."
"I began to work at a very early age, I never asked anyone for anything. Since I was young, I have slept five hours a night. I believe I have achieved something."
"When I receive a letter, I always reply within 48 hours unless, of course, I am travelling."

Havelange said that Pele, who appeared on the international scene at the age of 17 with a spectacular performance in the 1958 World Cup in Sweden, would never have played in the tournament without his backing.

Havelange, who compared FIFA to the United Nations at every available opportunity and continually referred to the organisation's statutes, was an official in the Brazilian Sports Confederation (CBD) at the time.
"I have always treated him like a son. Get any newspaper of the time and you will see that in 1958, when he was 17, I was violently criticised for taking a child to play football."
"But he became the greatest player in the world because he went and as a result he gained an extra four years. I have always tried to develop his qualities."
Waving a copy of FIFA's statute book, Havelange said he was merely trying to do his duty as president of world soccer's governing body.
"My obligation is to defend the statutes of the entity of which I am president," he said. "I am not here to go the against the president of the republic, who I respect and who is my friend."
"We have had cases with Germany, England and Greece and they have always ended up respecting the statutes."
Pele's bill intends to make club directors more accountable and referees and disciplinary tribunals independent from the CBF.

Many Brazilian clubs are in financial trouble, crowds at the majority of domestic games are paltry and fixture lists are crushing. Organisation of the domestic game is chaotic with a multitude of competitions which often overlap with each other, while violence on the field is a major problem.
Havelange, however, concentrated on the other side of the coin -- the national team, which has won a record-breaking four World Cups.
"Football is better organised than anything else in the country. It has brought glories, victories and happiness to the people," he said.
"Sport in Brazil is not just football. There's rowing, basketball, volleyball and we don't do anything for them."
"The CBF does not receive any money from the government....The players are always paid, they travel in the best conditions, and the (CBF) building doesn't cost anything because I gave it to them."
